steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a short paper proposing an iterative cycle for assessing and improving the operational accuracy of DNN classifiers. Explain why pre-release accuracy estimates are not enough and how pseudo-oracles and sampling-based assessment can be combined, then summarize preliminary results and the paper structure.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. ML/DNN adoption and accuracy as reliability measure
2. Pre-release assessment vs. operational accuracy
3. Iterative DNN life cycles (MLOps)
4. The oracle problem and two assessment approaches
5. Proposal: DAIC and preliminary results
6. Paper structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Adoption
- ML widely adopted across domains; DNNs reach human effectiveness in many tasks
- reliability measured as accuracy; classification: correctly classified / total
- hard to automate accuracy assessment -> threat to use in critical domains

2. Pre-release vs. operation
- evaluation + improvement usually before release
- metamorphic testing, mutation testing: most common for robustness / forecasting operational reliability
- pre-release accuracy can diverge from operational accuracy
- Retch et al.: accuracy drops significantly on completely new data
- worse with distribution shift or label shift

3. Iterative life cycles
- MLOps, envisaged by companies like Google
- development and operation linked in a loop; assess + improve accuracy per operating conditions
- operational data for remodeling/retraining before new deployment (experimental stage); automatic accuracy evaluation + automatic re-training on the field (deployment stage)

4. Oracle problem
- true label of monitored operational data generally unknown = oracle problem
- [quote: Murphy et al. on no reliable test oracle for ML]
- affects DNN accuracy estimation
- approach i) pseudo-oracles (often ML-based) detect mispredictions from various knowledge sources
- approach ii) statistical sampling of few representative inputs to reduce labelling
- pseudo-oracles: no human, but many false positives (probabilistic knowledge)
- sampling: reduces but doesn't avoid human feedback; no false positives, more faithful estimates

5. DAIC
- DNN Assessment and Improvement Cycle: pseudo-oracles + sampling
- goals: faithful operational accuracy estimates, less manual cost; use new labeled examples to remodel/retrain
- MNIST handwritten digits: effective estimates; pseudo-oracles follow accuracy on unlabeled samples; costly sampling only when needed; samples reused to improve DNN in iteration; robust to label shift

6. Structure
- II techniques; III DAIC; IV preliminary results; V future plans; VI conclusions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Nowadays Machine Learning (ML) is widely adopted in many application domains. This is because ML, and in particular Deep Neural Networks (DNN), can reach the effectiveness of human beings in many tasks.

The reliability of ML systems is usually measured as accuracy. For classification, accuracy is the number of correctly classified examples out of the total. It is still difficult to automate the assessment of DNN accuracy, and this is a threat to using them also in critical domains.

The main activities for evaluating the accuracy, and so improving the DNN, are usually done before it is released into the execution environment. Metamorphic testing and mutation testing are the most common strategies to evaluate the robustness of the DNN and forecast how reliable these systems will be in the operational environment.

But the accuracy estimated before release can be very different from the accuracy obtained during operation (operational accuracy). Retch et al. showed that the accuracy scores of classifiers can drop significantly when completely new data are submitted. This problem gets bigger when unexpected phenomena happen in operation, like distribution shift or label shift.

Companies like Google have envisaged iterative life cycles specific for DNN, such as MLOps. In these DNN life cycle models the development and operational stages are linked in a loop, with the aim of assessing and improving the accuracy of the DNN according to the operating conditions. In particular they may use operational data to remodel and/or retrain the DNN before the new deployment (experimental stage), and both to automatically evaluate the accuracy and to automatically re-train the models on the field (deployment stage).

The true label of the operational data collected by monitoring the DNN is usually unknown. This is a general issue in software testing which is known as the oracle problem. For ML systems, Murphy et al. say that “ there is no reliable test oracle to indicate what the correct output should be for arbitrary input ”. Clearly the problem also affects DNN accuracy estimation.

There are two approaches to assess DNN operational accuracy:

- i) to automatically evaluate whether operational inputs are classified correctly by using pseudo-oracles (which are often based on ML models themselves), which may detect mispredictions based on various sources of knowledge;

- ii) to reduce the size of the operational dataset that has to be labelled, by statistically sampling a few representative inputs.

Pseudo-oracles do not need human intervention, but they usually have a high number of false positives, because the knowledge used to evaluate the output of the DNN under assessment is probabilistic. Sampling techniques can reduce, but not avoid, costly and time-consuming feedback from a human oracle; but they avoid false positives and give more faithful estimates of the DNN operational accuracy.

In this paper we propose the DNN Assessment and Improvement Cycle (DAIC), which integrates automatic assessment via pseudo-oracles and assessment via sampling. The objectives are to give faithful estimates of the operational accuracy of a DNN while reducing the cost of manual intervention, and to use the new labeled examples to take remodeling/retraining actions that improve the DNN accuracy.

The preliminary results of experiments with the MNIST handwritten digits dataset show that DAIC is effective in giving DNN accuracy estimates. It uses automatic pseudo-oracles to follow the accuracy of the DNN with unlabeled samples, and it triggers the high-cost sampling-based assessment only when it is necessary to update the estimates. The collected operational samples are then also used to improve the accuracy of the DNN in an iteration cycle. DAIC is robust to phenomena like label shift.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II describes techniques for operational accuracy assessment of DNN. Section III introduces the DNN Assessment and Improvement Cycle. Section IV presents the preliminary results. Section V describes future plans, and Section VI presents the conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Nowadays, Machine Learning (ML) is widely adopted in various application domains. This trend is due to the ability of ML, in particular of Deep Neural Networks (DNN), to reach human beings’ effectiveness in many tasks [1,2,3].

The reliability of ML systems is usually measured in terms of accuracy. In the case of classification, the accuracy is computed as the number of correctly classified examples out of the total. The difficulty of automating the assessment of DNN accuracy still represents a threat to their application, also in critical domains.

The main activities related to evaluating the accuracy, and consequently improving the DNN, are typically executed before its release in the execution environment. Metamorphic testing [4] and mutation testing [5,6] are the most common strategies to evaluate the robustness of the DNN and to forecast the reliability of these systems in the operational environment.

However, the accuracy estimated before release can substantially diverge from the one obtained during operation (operational accuracy). Retch et al. demonstrated that the accuracy scores of classifiers can significantly drop when completely new data are submitted [7]. This problem grows when unexpected phenomena occur in operation, such as distribution shift or label shift [8].

Iterative life cycles specific for DNN, such as MLOps [9,10], have been envisaged by companies like Google. In these DNN life cycle models, development and operational stages are linked in a loop [11], aiming to assess and improve the accuracy of the DNN according to the operating conditions. In particular, they may exploit operational data for remodeling and/or retraining the DNN before the new deployment (experimental stage), and for both the automatic evaluation of the accuracy and the automatic re-training of the models on the field (deployment stage).

The true label of operational data collected by monitoring the DNN is generally unknown. This is a general issue in software testing, known as the oracle problem [12]. For ML systems, according to Murphy et al., “ there is no reliable test oracle to indicate what the correct output should be for arbitrary input ” [13]. The problem clearly also affects DNN accuracy estimation [14].

Two approaches to assess DNN operational accuracy are:

- i) to automatically evaluate the correct classification of operational inputs by means of pseudo-oracles (often themselves based on ML models), which may detect mispredictions based on various sources of knowledge;

- ii) to reduce the size of the operational dataset to be labelled, by statistical sampling of a few representative inputs.

Pseudo-oracles do not need human intervention; however, they typically suffer from a high number of false positives [15], due to the probabilistic nature of the knowledge used to evaluate the output of the DNN under assessment. Sampling techniques may reduce but not avoid costly and time-consuming feedback from a human oracle; however, they avoid false positives and provide more faithful estimates of the DNN operational accuracy.

This paper proposes the DNN Assessment and Improvement Cycle (DAIC), which integrates automatic assessment via pseudo-oracles and assessment via sampling. Its objectives are to provide faithful estimates of the operational accuracy of a DNN while reducing the cost of manual intervention, and to exploit the new labeled examples to take remodeling/retraining actions that improve the DNN accuracy.

The preliminary results of experiments with the MNIST handwritten digits dataset [16] show that DAIC is effective in providing DNN accuracy estimates: it leverages automatic pseudo-oracles to follow the accuracy of the DNN with unlabeled samples, and triggers the high-cost sampling-based assessment only when necessary to update estimates. The collected operational samples are then further exploited to improve the accuracy of the DNN in an iteration cycle. DAIC is robust to phenomena like label shift.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II describes the techniques for the operational accuracy assessment of DNN. Section III introduces the DNN Assessment and Improvement Cycle; Section IV presents the preliminary results. Section V describes future plans, and Section VI presents the conclusions.
